Our Cookies, and the Stories Behind Them

Real ingredients, New England history, and a full 1/4 LB in every cookie. These are the stories behind the six cookies we bake, told the way we would tell them across the counter.

Top seller

Chocolate Chip: a flavor story

The Cookie That Outsells Every Other Cookie We Bake

Chocolate Chip is our top seller at every location, according to our Square sales data, and not by a little.

There is a reason, and it is not complicated.

Sweet and buttery, with loads of chocolate chips

That is the house description, and it is exact. The dough is sweet and buttery: real butter, real sugar, the way a chocolate chip cookie was meant to be built. Then the chips: loads of them, in every bite, not a polite scattering you have to hunt for. It is a full 1/4 LB of cookie, thick and chewy, with a toasty outer layer that gives way to a soft center.

This is the cookie by which every other chocolate chip cookie gets judged. We know that. So we bake it like it.

Why it wins

  1. Real ingredients, no fillers. We don’t use cheap or artificial filler products. Butter is butter. Sugar is sugar. You taste the difference in the first bite and you remember it in the tenth.
  2. A quarter pound, not a suggestion of one. Each cookie weighs a full 1/4 LB. It is thick. It is chewy. It eats like a dessert, because it is one.
  3. The toasty outer layer. A proper old-fashioned cookie has structure: a lightly toasted exterior that gives way to a chewy middle. That contrast is the whole experience, and it only happens when the bake is watched, not rushed.

The story behind it

This one has a birth certificate, and it was issued in Massachusetts.

In 1930, Ruth Graves Wakefield, a trained dietitian, and her husband opened the Toll House Inn in Whitman, south of Boston. Around 1938, she chopped a Nestlé semi-sweet chocolate bar into bits and folded them into drop-cookie dough. The bits held their shape in the oven instead of melting through. She named it the “Toll House Chocolate Crunch Cookie” and printed the recipe in 1938, the first printed chocolate-chip cookie recipe, according to the Library of Congress.

In 1939, Nestlé bought the rights for a dollar and a lifetime supply of chocolate. Massachusetts soldiers got the cookies in care packages during World War II. The inn burned down in 1984. The cookie did not.

Eighty-eight years after Whitman, we’re still baking the Massachusetts original, at a full 1/4 LB, with loads of chips in every bite. There is a reason it still wins, and the reason is the recipe.

What “old-fashioned” means here

“Old-fashioned” gets printed on a lot of packages. Here it means something specific: a cookie made the way it would have been made before the 1950s, in its ingredients, in its process, and in the flavors themselves, which were created here in New England.

The ingredients are the traditional ones. Premium lard, the fat New England kitchens baked with for generations, worked together with real butter: that combination is what gives our cookies their unique flavor and texture. Real ingredients, honestly stated: no artificial flavors doing the work that real ingredients should do, no fillers stretching the dough. The process has not changed either: dough portioned at a full quarter pound, baked pan by pan, batch by batch, by a baker who knows what done looks like: a lightly toasted exterior giving way to a thick, chewy center.

That’s the standard behind every cookie we bake. That’s what “old-fashioned” means here.

We make five core flavors, and every one of them has its devoted following. The Chocolate Chip just happens to be the one that outsells them all.

Molasses

Molasses: a flavor story

Long before white sugar was cheap and everywhere, New England baked with molasses. It came up the coast on trading ships, and it went into brown bread, baked beans, gingerbread, and the dark, chewy cookies that grandmothers made when company was coming.

A molasses cookie done right is not a spice cookie with only a hint of molasses in it. Ours is built on real molasses, the dark, full-flavored kind, folded through a buttery dough with the warm spices that belong beside it. A full 1/4 LB of it.

Read the full story
  1. Real molasses. The deep sweetness in this cookie comes from actual molasses in the dough, the whole story in every bite.
  2. The old New England spice balance. Warm spices, measured the way they have been measured for generations, present, never shouting. The molasses leads. Everything else follows.
  3. Chewy by construction. Molasses holds moisture, which is the baker’s way of saying this cookie stays soft and chewy the way it should.

In the 1700s, molasses from Caribbean sugar plantations poured into New England ports. Boston alone had more than 25 rum distilleries by mid-century. When white sugar was expensive and molasses was what a household had, molasses sweetened brown bread, baked beans, and gingerbread: the backbone of the colonial New England table. The dark, chewy molasses cookie is a direct descendant of that kitchen.

Oatmeal Raisin

Oatmeal Raisin: a flavor story

The oatmeal raisin cookie has been misunderstood for decades. It can get less attention than the chocolate chip, until somebody tries it. The Oatmeal Raisin deserves better than its reputation. Here is the defense it deserves.

Start with hearty oats that give the cookie its substantial, satisfying chew. Add plump raisins, soft and sweet all the way through. Bind it with a buttery dough warmed with real cinnamon. Bake it thick, a full 1/4 LB, to a toasty outer layer with a chewy center.

Read the full story
  1. The raisins are the point, not the garnish. Ours are plump and generous, in every bite. A raisin should taste like something. These do.
  2. Oats give it a chew nothing else has. The hearty oat texture is the signature of this cookie, substantial in a way a plain butter cookie never is.
  3. It is the best cookie in the lineup with a cup of coffee. It holds up to dunking. Thick enough to survive the dip. Flavorful enough to deserve it.

In 1896, Fannie Merritt Farmer, principal of the Boston Cooking School, published The Boston Cooking-School Cook Book: one of the earliest published oatmeal cookie recipes in the United States. Our Oatmeal Raisin honors that lineage the honest way: real hearty oats, plump raisins in every bite, real cinnamon, real butter, real brown sugar, baked thick at a full 1/4 LB.

Coffee Cake

Coffee Cake: a flavor story

Somewhere along the way, somebody asked the obvious question: what if the best part of coffee cake, the tender, buttery crumb, the cinnamon streusel, the sweet drizzle, came in a thick, chewy, quarter-pound cookie? This is the answer.

Our Coffee Cake cookie starts with a soft, cake-like cookie base, tender and buttery, the way good coffee cake is tender. Then it gets the full treatment: a crumbly brown-sugar streusel baked right across the top, and a sweet icing drizzle to finish.

Read the full story
  1. It is two desserts in one, honestly built. The streusel is mixed and baked onto the cookie, finished with a sweet icing drizzle. Every layer is real, and every layer is there for a reason.
  2. The texture contrast is the whole point. Tender cookie beneath, crumbly streusel above, smooth icing over all of it. Three textures in every bite.
  3. It pairs with coffee the way it was born to. A medium-roast coffee alongside this cookie is one of the finest simple pleasures in New England.

It starts in Germany, with the kaffeekuchen, literally “coffee cake,” and its signature streusel: the German word means “sprinkle” or “strew.” German and Dutch immigrants carried the tradition to America in the mid-1800s. Some flavors inherit their history. This one inherited its ingredients’ history and is writing its own, in a Manchester, New Hampshire kitchen, one 1/4 LB cookie at a time.

Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip

Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip: a flavor story

Peanut butter and chocolate is not a combination that needed improving. It needed room. A full quarter pound of room, to be exact.

Our Peanut Butter Chocolate Chip takes two of the most beloved flavors in American baking and bakes them into one thick, chewy, 1/4 LB cookie with the toasty outer layer that marks everything we make. Sweet meets salty. Soft center meets toasty edge.

Read the full story
  1. Peanut butter, full measure. The peanut flavor in this cookie comes from real peanut butter in the dough. Rich, salty, and unmistakable.
  2. Loads of chocolate chips. They are distributed through the whole quarter pound, so the chocolate-to-peanut-butter ratio holds from the first bite to the last.
  3. The salt-sweet balance is deliberate. A great peanut butter cookie walks a line: rich and sweet, but with enough salt to keep it interesting. That balance is in the recipe on purpose.

Peanut cookies go back further than most people think: George Washington Carver published peanut cookie recipes in a 1916 research bulletin. The signature fork-pressed crosshatch first appeared in print in a 1932 newspaper recipe. The press was never decoration: peanut butter dough is dense, and flattening it helps it bake evenly.

Pumpkin Maple-Pecan Crunch

The fall seasonal

Available through November 30, 2026

There is a short list of flavors that belong to a New England fall. Pumpkin. Maple. Pecan. Together, in a thick, chewy, quarter-pound cookie, they are the season itself.

Real pumpkin gives the cookie its moist, tender crumb and its warm autumn color. Pecans, crunchy and buttery, are folded through the dough so every bite has texture. And the finish: a maple-glaze drizzle laid across the top of every cookie.

Read the full story
  1. Pumpkin done properly. Real pumpkin in the dough, the right spice measure, and a watched bake. Moist and tender, never gummy, never dry.
  2. Crunch where it counts. The pecans earn the “crunch” in the name. Buttery, distributed through the whole quarter pound.
  3. The maple-glaze drizzle. A real maple drizzle makes the pumpkin and pecan underneath taste even more like themselves.

Maple is the older story still. Long before European colonists arrived, the Indigenous peoples of the Northeast were making maple sugar: tapping in the freeze-thaw weeks of late winter, boiling the sap down to syrup. In New England, maple is a heritage, and the glaze puts that heritage front and center on every cookie.
